content:
Should a local business pay Google for clicks on its own name? It is one of the first questions a digital marketing agency in Pune gets from a client who has just seen the search terms report and noticed that a large share of "conversions" came from people typing the business name. The honest answer is: sometimes. Bidding on your own brand is worth it when competitors, directories or resellers appear above you for your name, when you need control over the message (an offer, a new branch, a booking link), or when your organic listing is weak. It is often wasted money when you already own the whole first screen for your name and nobody else is bidding. The way to know which applies to you is not opinion but a simple test, which this guide explains along with how to set up a brand campaign properly, how to stop brand clicks from inflating your other campaigns' results, and what to do when a competitor bids on your name.

The advice here applies to service businesses, clinics, institutes, retailers and e-commerce stores running Google Ads. It does not give legal advice on trademarks; where the law matters, we say so.

## What "brand bidding" means

A brand campaign targets searches that contain your business name or your product names: "Sharma Dental Kothrud", "sharma dental appointment", "sharmadental.in". Because the searcher already knows you, these clicks usually cost little and convert well. That is precisely why they can mislead you: a brand campaign will almost always show a low cost per lead and a high conversion rate, but much of that demand would have reached you anyway through your organic listing or Google Business Profile.

The question is therefore not "do brand ads convert?" (they do) but "how many of those conversions would I lose if I stopped?" That is called incrementality.

## The case for bidding on your own name

### 1. Others are bidding on it

Look at the results page for your name on a phone, in incognito mode, a few times over a week and from different locations in Pune. If you see a competitor's ad, an aggregator, a booking platform, a directory listing or a reseller above your organic result, someone is buying attention that was meant for you. A brand ad puts you back at the top. This is the most common and most defensible reason to run one.

### 2. Your organic result is not good enough

New websites, recently rebranded businesses and firms whose name is a common word often do not rank first for their own name, or rank with an unhelpful page (an old blog post rather than the home page). Until the website's search presence is fixed, a brand ad ensures searchers land on the right page. Fixing the underlying SEO should still be the priority; see our [SEO services](/services/seo).

### 3. You need control over the message

An organic listing shows a title and description that Google may rewrite. An ad lets you say exactly what you want: "Now open in Baner", "Admissions open for 2027", "Festive offer till 31 October", plus sitelinks to booking, pricing and directions. For time-sensitive messages, the control is worth paying for.

### 4. Screen space on mobile

On a phone, an ad with sitelinks, a call asset and a location asset can fill most of the first screen. That reduces the chance that the searcher taps a competitor or a review site instead. Whether that space is worth the money is again a matter of testing.

## The case against

### 1. You may be paying for clicks you would get free

If nobody else appears for your name and you rank first organically with a strong Google Business Profile, a brand ad mostly takes clicks your organic listing would have received. You pay for traffic you already had.

### 2. It flatters the account

When brand and non-brand searches share a campaign, the cheap, high-converting brand clicks hide how the expensive non-brand keywords are really performing. A campaign that looks profitable overall may be losing money on every non-brand lead. This is the most damaging effect and the reason we always separate brand from non-brand, whether or not we keep the brand campaign running.

### 3. Automated campaigns drift towards brand

Performance Max and broad-match search campaigns with automated bidding look for the cheapest conversions they can find. Unless told otherwise, they will often serve on brand searches, because brand converts easily. The report then credits the automated campaign with sales that your name generated. Google provides brand exclusions to prevent this (see below).

## How to test whether brand ads are worth it

You do not need a data science team. You need a clean before-and-after or, better, an on/off test.

**Step 1: Gather a baseline.** For at least four weeks, record for brand searches: ad clicks, ad conversions, organic clicks for brand queries from Google Search Console (filter queries containing your name), and total leads or sales from all sources in your CRM or sheet. Our guide to [Search Console striking-distance queries](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-search-console-striking-distance-queries-ctr-2026) shows how to filter queries.

**Step 2: Pause, or reduce, for a defined period.** Pause the brand campaign for two to four weeks. If you are nervous, pause it only on some days of the week or in some locations, and compare.

**Step 3: Compare totals, not channel reports.** The question is whether total brand-originated leads (ads plus organic plus direct calls) fell, and by how much. If organic clicks rose to cover most of the lost ad clicks and total leads held steady, the brand campaign was mostly paying for traffic you would have had. If total leads fell, or a competitor's ad started appearing in your place, the campaign was doing real work.

**Step 4: Decide and recheck.** Re-run the check every few months or when something changes: a new competitor, a rebrand, a big campaign push.

Two caveats. First, small businesses have small numbers; a difference of three or four leads in a month may be noise. Run the test long enough to see a pattern, and pay attention to what appears on the results page while you are paused. Second, seasonality matters. Do not compare a festive month with a quiet one.

## Setting up a brand campaign properly

If you decide to run one, keep it separate and keep it tight.

### Campaign structure

- **One search campaign for brand only.** Name it clearly, for example "Search | Brand | Pune".
- **Ad groups by intent if you have several brands or products.** For a single-location business, one ad group is often enough.
- **Keywords:** your name in exact and phrase match, common misspellings, the name with locality ("Kothrud", "Baner"), the domain name if people type it into search, and product or service names that are unique to you.
- **Negative keywords:** words that indicate the searcher wants something other than a customer relationship: "jobs", "careers", "salary", "internship", "complaint" (you may prefer to handle complaints organically), and names of similarly named but unrelated businesses. Our guide to [negative keywords and the search terms report](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-negative-keywords-search-terms-report-2026) covers how to find them.

### Ads and assets

- Headlines that confirm identity and give the next step: your name, "Official Website", the main service, the locality, and a clear action such as "Book an Appointment".
- Sitelinks to the pages people search your name to find: contact, pricing, booking, branches, specific services.
- Call asset with your main number and call reporting turned on, and a location asset linked to your Google Business Profile.
- Make sure any claim in the ad (offers, timings) matches the landing page.

### Bidding and budget

Brand clicks are usually cheap because your ad is highly relevant to the search and your landing page matches it. Quality Score for brand keywords tends to be high; our guide to [Quality Score and Ad Rank](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-quality-score-ad-rank-cost-per-click-2026) explains why. Set a modest daily budget and watch impression share: if you are not showing for a large share of your own brand searches because of budget, raise it slightly. If cost per click on your own name starts rising sharply, that usually means someone else is competing for it.

Avoid letting a fully automated strategy chase brand conversions with an unlimited target. A manual or capped approach is usually enough for a brand campaign; your aim is to appear, not to win an auction at any price.

### Keep brand out of everything else

- **Add your brand terms as negative keywords** in non-brand search campaigns, so those campaigns are judged on genuine new demand.
- **Use brand exclusions** for Performance Max and, where available, for Search campaigns using broad match or AI Max. Google lets you create brand lists in the shared library and exclude them from campaigns; check the current help page because the options for Search campaigns changed in 2025 and are now tied to AI Max settings on new campaigns.
- **Report brand and non-brand separately** to the business owner. A monthly report that mixes them hides the true cost of new customers.

## When a competitor bids on your name

This is common in competitive local categories in Pune: clinics, coaching classes, interiors, real estate, salons. It feels unfair, but you have fewer options than people expect.

### What Google's policy says

Google's trademark policy, as published, does not prevent advertisers from using a trademark as a keyword in most countries. It can restrict the use of a trademark in the text of an ad after a valid complaint by the owner. In other words, a competitor may be allowed to bid on your name, but if your name is a registered trademark and you file a complaint, Google may stop them from using it in the ad copy. Check Google's current trademark policy and complaint process for India before you act; it is updated from time to time.

### What Indian courts have said

Indian courts, particularly the Delhi High Court, have considered whether using another company's registered trademark as a keyword is infringement, and the outcomes have depended on the facts of each case. The legal position is not settled in a way that a blog article can summarise safely. If a competitor's keyword bidding is causing you real harm, speak to a trademark lawyer; do not rely on a marketing agency's opinion.

### Practical steps that usually help more

1. **Run your own brand campaign** so you appear above or alongside them. Your ad will usually be more relevant than theirs, so it often costs you less per click.
2. **Strengthen your Google Business Profile**: complete categories, fresh photos, accurate hours and a steady flow of genuine reviews. A strong profile is the main thing many local searchers see.
3. **File a trademark complaint with Google** if your name is registered and their ad text uses it.
4. **Do not retaliate blindly.** Bidding on competitors' names can bring cheap clicks, but conversion rates are usually low, the ads cannot use their trademark in the text after a complaint, and it may invite the same legal questions. If you do test it, measure it separately and stop if it does not produce leads at an acceptable cost.

## Special cases

### E-commerce stores

For online stores, brand searches often include product names ("[brand] cotton kurta") and the store's own shopping results may already appear. Performance Max and Shopping campaigns will serve on brand searches unless excluded. Keep a separate brand search campaign, apply brand exclusions to Performance Max where appropriate, and judge the shopping campaigns on non-brand sales.

### Franchises and multi-location businesses

If franchisees run their own ads, they may compete with the head office for the same brand searches, raising everyone's cost. Agree in writing who bids on what: head office on the main brand, each branch on "brand + locality", with shared negative keywords.

### Resellers and distributors

Manufacturers often find that distributors bid on the manufacturer's brand. Whether that helps or hurts depends on the relationship. Write it into the distributor agreement rather than discovering it in the search results.

### New or renamed businesses

For the first months after a launch or rebrand, a brand campaign is usually justified while your website builds organic visibility for the new name. Plan to test pausing it once the site ranks first.

## What a sensible monthly brand report looks like

Ask your agency for these numbers, separately from non-brand:

- Brand impressions and impression share (how often you appeared for your own name).
- Brand clicks, cost and cost per click, with a note if cost per click is rising.
- Brand conversions, labelled as such and excluded from "cost per new lead" calculations.
- Organic clicks for brand queries from Search Console, to see the combined picture.
- Any competitors seen in auction insights for brand terms.
- Any action taken (new negatives, trademark complaints, budget changes) and why.

If your report does not separate brand from non-brand, ask for that before anything else. Our guide to [testing budgets across Google Ads and Meta Ads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-meta-ads-testing-budget-2026) explains how to judge the non-brand side.

## An illustrative example

Consider a physiotherapy clinic in Pune with two branches. Its single Google Ads campaign reports a low cost per appointment request. When the agency splits the campaign, most of the cheap conversions turn out to come from people searching the clinic's name. The non-brand keywords ("physiotherapist near me", "back pain treatment Kothrud") cost several times more per enquiry than the blended figure suggested. The clinic keeps a small brand campaign because a larger hospital chain's ad was appearing for its name, adds brand terms as negatives elsewhere, and rewrites the non-brand landing pages. This is an invented example to show the method, not a description of a real client.

## How Govindani approaches brand campaigns

When we take over a Google Ads account, one of the first things we do is separate brand from non-brand and show the owner what new customers actually cost. Whether we keep a brand campaign running depends on what appears for the client's name and on the results of a pause test, not on a rule of thumb. ## Frequently asked questions

### Should I bid on my own brand name in Google Ads?
Bid on it if competitors, directories or resellers appear above you for your name, if your organic result is weak, or if you need to control the message. If nobody else appears and you already rank first, test pausing the brand campaign and compare total leads before deciding.

### Why are brand keywords so cheap?
Your ad is highly relevant to someone searching your name, the landing page matches and people click it readily, so your Quality Score is high and you need to bid less to appear. If brand costs per click start rising, someone is likely competing for your name.

### Can a competitor legally bid on my business name in India?
Google's policy generally allows trademarks as keywords but can restrict their use in ad text after a complaint. Indian courts have looked at keyword use of trademarks case by case and the law is not settled. For a specific dispute, consult a trademark lawyer.

### How do I stop Performance Max from taking credit for brand searches?
Create a brand list in the Google Ads shared library and apply it as a brand exclusion to the Performance Max campaign, then run a separate brand search campaign. Check Google's current help page, as brand controls for Search campaigns changed in 2025.

### Should brand and non-brand be in the same campaign?
No. Mixing them makes non-brand performance look better than it is, because cheap brand conversions lower the average cost per lead. Keep them in separate campaigns and report them separately.
